transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Luis Quivoni.
Mexican authorities say they have captured one of the most wanted drug lords in the country.
NPR's Ada Peralta reports he was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list.
Fausto Isidro Mesaflores, who was better known as El Chapo Isidro, is the leader of the Beltran Leyva cartel.
The U.S. accuses him of running huge quantities of drugs, including meth and fentanyl, to the U.S.
The Mexican military says it captured Mesaflores in Wasave, Sinaloa, using U.S. intelligence.
Residents reported that the military fired from helicopters while the cartels burned cars and trucks.
A baseball game was disrupted by the heavy fighting, and some residents had to spend the night at a supermarket to stay safe.
Over the past couple of years, as the U.S. has mounted pressure on Mexico to fight organized crime,
security forces have captured a number of drug lords.
The power vacuums have often led to an increase in violence.
Ada Peralta, NPR News, Mexico City.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie says that on guidance from the National Weather Service and NOAA,
who are forecasting high tides and heavy rain, he's encouraging people not to travel over the coming Thanksgiving week.
I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday,
but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential starting Monday afternoon
and going into Wednesday afternoon.
We are expecting tides that the National Weather Service told us they have never seen before in recorded history here in San Francisco.
On the east coast, a storm is forming off Florida's Atlantic shores with the potential of strengthening into a tropical or subtropical storm.
The system is expected to move north into Georgia, the Carolinas and the middle Atlantic states.
AAA forecasts 81.5 million people in the U.S. will be traveling this holiday week.
A final draft of a climate agreement at UN COP 31 talks in Antalya, Turkey has failed to mention the impact of fossil fuels on global warming,
leading international delegates to add another day to their deliberations.
NPR's Rachel Waldoats has more from Antalya.
Many of the countries that have been most affected by climate change,
they want the agreement that comes out of Antalya to explicitly state that it's necessary for the world to transition away from fossil fuels.
And oil-producing countries, notably Saudi Arabia and Russia, they're resisting that language.
Burning fossil fuels like coal and oil and natural gas, it's the primary driver of climate change.
It is also the key to the global economy, and so it's always a delicate issue.
NPR's Rachel Waldoats reporting.
Agri-chemical company Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company,
alleging the weed killer Roundup caused their cancer.
A judge in Missouri approved the settlement this week.
This is NPR News.
As a new Democratic-controlled Congress prepares to convene within the next two months,
President Trump is bracing for inquiries with a new executive order directing contractors
who've done business with the administration to consult with Trump's team before talking to lawmakers.
The new Hunger Games movie is off to a fast start at the box office, and NPR's Bob Mondello has details.
It's a pretty safe bet that with these dystopian films about a society that forces children to battle to the death...
The arena. It's a killing machine.
Box office odds are ever in your favor.
The previous Hunger Games installments have collectively taken in $3.3 billion at the box office,
and this sixth quell, which is being sold as having...
Twice the number of tributes, twice the glory.
...appears likely to continue the winning streak with a hefty $120 million in North America this weekend
and another $100 million overseas.
We're not animals to kill for their entertainment.
Hunger Games' Sunrise on the Reaping is kicking off what's expected to be a killer holiday season for Hollywood,
one that will cap a $10 billion year for the first time since COVID disrupted the entertainment industry in 2020.
Bob Mondello, NPR News.
Mathematical problem that's lingered for more than one and a half centuries appears to have been solved
in a researcher at Anthropic as giving the credit to the company's AI chatbot, Claude.
The Riemann hypothesis addresses how prime numbers are spread out.
The mathematician at Anthropic says Claude made it through the final parts of the problem.
Final verification is pending.
I'm Louise Schiavone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Mexican military captures Beltran Leyva cartel leader Fausto Isidro Mesaflores, known as El Chapo Isidro
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie urges residents to avoid travel during Thanksgiving week due to tides and rain
Storm forming off Florida's Atlantic coast could strengthen into tropical or subtropical storm
UN COP 31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey extended a day over fossil fuel language in draft agreement
Bayer agrees to pay billions to settle lawsuits alleging Roundup weed killer caused cancer; Missouri judge approves
Trump issues executive order requiring contractors to consult his team before talking to incoming Democratic Congress
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens strongly at the box office, expected to earn $120 million domestically
Anthropic researcher says its Claude AI chatbot helped solve the Riemann hypothesis, verification pending
